final_proof:
We use the standard convention that a smooth manifold is Hausdorff and second countable; the argument also works if one-manifolds with boundary are allowed. Choose a diffeomorphism from an open interval onto \(L\), and precompose it with a diffeomorphism from \((0,1)\) onto that interval. We thus have a continuous injective map

\[
f:(0,1)\longrightarrow X
\]

whose image is \(L\).

We first prove an end-uniqueness lemma. Let \(M\) be a Hausdorff one-manifold, possibly with boundary, and let \(h:(0,1)\to M\) be continuous and injective. We claim that there cannot be distinct points \(p,q\in M\) and sequences \(r_n,s_n\to1\) such that \(h(r_n)\to p\) and \(h(s_n)\to q\).

Suppose otherwise. Choose a sufficiently small coordinate interval \(U\) about \(p\) such that \(q\notin\overline U\) and the boundary of \(U\) in \(M\) has at most two points. Such a choice is possible by taking a smaller interval whose closure is contained in a coordinate chart: its boundary has two points if \(p\) is an interior point of \(M\), and one point if \(p\) is a boundary point. Put \(V=M\setminus\overline U\), which is an open neighborhood of \(q\).

The assumed convergences imply that every terminal interval \((c,1)\) contains a parameter mapped into \(U\) and a parameter mapped into \(V\). Hence we may choose

\[
a_1<b_1<a_2<b_2<a_3<b_3<1
\]

so that \(h(a_i)\in U\) and \(h(b_i)\in V\) for \(i=1,2,3\). For each \(i\), define

\[
c_i=\sup\{t\in[a_i,b_i]:h(t)\in U\}.
\]

The set in this definition is nonempty. Also \(c_i<b_i\): otherwise there would be points \(t\) mapped into \(U\) arbitrarily close to \(b_i\), and continuity would imply \(h(b_i)\in\overline U\), contrary to \(h(b_i)\in V\). By the definition of the supremum and continuity, \(h(c_i)\in\overline U\). But \(h(c_i)\notin U\), since otherwise the open set \(h^{-1}(U)\) would contain a parameter slightly larger than \(c_i\) and still less than \(b_i\), contradicting the definition of \(c_i\). Therefore

\[
h(c_i)\in\partial U \qquad (i=1,2,3).
\]

The intervals \([a_i,b_i]\) are pairwise disjoint, so the three parameters \(c_i\) are distinct. Since \(h\) is injective, the three points \(h(c_i)\) are distinct. This contradicts \(|\partial U|\le2\), proving the lemma for the end \(1\). Applying the same lemma to \(t\mapsto h(1-t)\) proves it for the end \(0\) as well.

Now let \(x\in\overline L\setminus L\). Since \(X\) is first countable, there is a sequence \(x_n\in L\) with \(x_n\to x\). Write \(x_n=f(t_n)\), where \(t_n\in(0,1)\). Compactness of \([0,1]\) gives a subsequence of \((t_n)\) converging to some \(t\in[0,1]\). If \(t\in(0,1)\), then continuity gives \(f(t_n)\to f(t)\) along this subsequence. But the same sequence converges to \(x\), and the Hausdorff property makes limits unique. Thus \(x=f(t)\in L\), a contradiction. Consequently \(t=0\) or \(t=1\).

Therefore every point of \(\overline L\setminus L\) is approached through at least one of the two ends of \((0,1)\). By the end-uniqueness lemma, at most one such point can be approached through \(0\), and at most one through \(1\). Hence

\[
|\overline L\setminus L|\le2,
\]

as claimed.
